slides.label: Gauss's Theorema Egregium
slides.notes: Open by naming the surprise. Gaussian curvature was first introduced through the normal direction and the way a surface sits in three dimensional space, so it looks extrinsic. Gauss's theorem says the same number can be recovered from the surface's own metric data. The lecture question is therefore not whether curvature is useful, but why an outside-looking definition is secretly measurable from inside the surface.

slides.label: The Suspicious Definition
slides.notes: Before stating the theorem, remind the room why there is something to prove. Principal curvatures are found by watching normal sections bend in ambient space, and their product gives Gaussian curvature. That construction uses normals, osculating curves, and an outside viewer. The theorem will insist that after all of that extrinsic machinery has run, the final product depends only on the first fundamental form.

slides.label: Metric Data Is What an Inhabitant Measures
slides.notes: This slide fixes what intrinsic means operationally. An inhabitant can compare lengths, angles, areas, and geodesic distances using the metric coefficients E, F, and G. They do not need to know a normal vector in space. The ellipses in the local figure are a good visual proxy: each small ellipse tells how coordinate steps turn into physical lengths.

slides.label: Bending Without Stretching
slides.notes: Use the plane-to-cylinder example as the tactile model. A sheet rolled into a cylinder changes its normal directions and its visible embedding, but a rectangular grid drawn on the sheet keeps the same edge lengths and angles. Because the metric is unchanged, Theorema Egregium predicts the Gaussian curvature stays zero before and after the bending.

slides.label: The Theorem
slides.notes: State the theorem cleanly and slowly. If two surface patches are locally isometric, then their Gaussian curvatures agree at corresponding points. Equivalently, Gaussian curvature is determined by the first fundamental form and its derivatives. The word remarkable matters here because the definition seems to require the second fundamental form, while the theorem says the metric already contains the answer.

slides.label: How the Proof Can Possibly Work
slides.notes: Do not run a full symbolic proof on a slide. Instead give the roadmap: write the Levi-Civita connection from the metric, compute the curvature of that connection, and show the resulting scalar is the same Gaussian curvature obtained from the shape operator. This shows how extrinsic bending data gets eliminated and replaced by metric bookkeeping.

slides.label: Bending Versus Stretching
slides.notes: The contour figure separates two operations that can look similar in a picture. Bending alone changes the embedding but preserves the metric; stretching changes metric coefficients and therefore may change curvature. The red arrow is a reminder that once distances are actually rescaled, an intrinsic observer can detect the change without leaving the surface.

slides.label: Consequences for Maps
slides.notes: Now translate the theorem into a practical obstruction. A map that preserves all small lengths and angles must preserve Gaussian curvature. A plane and cylinder can be locally isometric because both have zero Gaussian curvature. A sphere cannot be flattened onto a plane without distortion because positive curvature cannot be carried to zero curvature by an isometry.

slides.label: Metric Determines Curvature Lab
slides.notes: Connect the theorem to the notebook's artifact checks. The computational pipeline starts from an object, builds a visual representation, writes the formula from metric coefficients, and records a sanity check. The important teaching point is not the particular implementation, but the invariant contract: the curvature computation should fail loudly if it depends on a chosen embedding rather than metric data.

slides.label: Takeaways
slides.notes: Close by returning to the chapter question. Gaussian curvature begins life as an outside measurement, but Gauss proved it is intrinsic. Bending without stretching preserves it; stretching can change it; and any length-preserving map must respect it. This is the hinge that turns curvature from a visual property of surfaces in space into a geometric invariant of the surface itself.
